content: NUBP2, also referred to as nucleotide-binding protein 2 or cytosolic Fe-S cluster assembly factor NUBP2, is a protein encoded by the NUBP2 gene in humans. This protein belongs to the NUBP/MRP gene subfamily, which is a group of ATP-binding proteins. In eukaryotes, there are two types of these proteins, NUBP1 and NUBP2, as well as a novel human gene that defines the NBP (nucleotide-binding protein) family. These proteins are associated with the maturation of cytosolic iron-sulfur (Fe/S) proteins. Specifically, NUBP1 is involved in the formation of extramitochondrial Fe/S proteins. The cell division inhibitor MinD is homologous to components of the Fe/S protein assembly machinery. This machinery includes two protein components that are closely related to cytosolic soluble P-loop NTPases. Nar1 is required for the assembly of these proteins, and Cfd1p has been identified as a key factor in the biogenesis of cytosolic and nuclear Fe/S proteins in yeast. NUBP proteins, including NTPase Nbp35p, play a critical role in this process. MinD is homologous to members of the MinD family in Escherichia coli, which is related to the ParA family of proteins. The NBP35 gene is conserved across a wide range of organisms, including archaea, bacteria, metazoa, fungi, and other eukaryotes, although it shows significant divergence from its yeast counterparts, such as Cfd1 and Nbp35. In humans, these proteins form part of a scaffold complex that assembles large molecular structures capable of storing Fe(III) and 4Fe-4S clusters. These structures are essential for the proper functioning of Fe/S proteins, which are physiologically relevant in various cellular processes. Iron regulatory protein 1 (IRP1) is one such Fe/S protein, and its activity is regulated to prevent deficiencies and mutations. These mutations are often associated with increased mutation rates and defects in Fe/S protein assembly. Additionally, a plant P-loop NTPase with sequence similarity to Nbp35 has been identified, further highlighting the evolutionary conservation and functional importance of these proteins.
